# Exercise 6.4 — For whom is the model worst? {#sec-subgroups}


::: {.callout-important}
## A suggested addition, not part of the original module
This exercise was proposed and drafted by the assistant that rebuilt the
booklet, not ported from an earlier version of the module. Exercise 1.2 Task 3 asked where a model is wrong; the question a service has to answer is for whom. The booklet measures performance on everyone at once and never splits it. Treat it as a
draft to accept, rewrite or delete: nothing else depends on it, and removing it
means deleting this file and its line in `_quarto.yml`.
:::

:::: {.web-only}
Every cell on this page is a real R or Python cell, run against
`data/diabetes.csv` with the Day 5.4 split.
::::

## Objectives

::: {.objective-list}
- Compute sensitivity, specificity and AUC inside subgroups of a test set, and
  report each one beside the number of rows and the number of cases it rests
  on.
- Build a noise floor for a between-group gap by permuting the group labels,
  and say whether an observed gap clears it.
- Explain why the group a subgroup table flags as worst served is usually the
  smallest one, and name what you would need to measure a real disparity.
:::

## Why this, here

@sec-importance, @sec-shap and @sec-dalex asked which variables the model used.
None of them asked who the model works for. Every metric in this booklet —
@sec-classification-metrics' AUC, @sec-thresholds' sensitivity, @sec-random-forest's
comparison table — has been computed on all 231 test rows at once, and a single
number over 231 people is an average over people who are not interchangeable.
@sec-pipeline asked where the model is wrong. A service has to answer a harder
version: for whom. This exercise splits the test set and asks that question,
and then spends most of its time on whether the answer means anything.

## Worked example — one model, scored on everyone

We audit the random forest of @sec-random-forest rather than the logistic
regression of @sec-logistic-regression, for one reason: it is the model Day 6
has spent all day explaining, and an equity audit in practice arrives after the
explanation, on the model somebody is proposing to deploy. Nothing in the
method depends on that choice — Stretch 1 repeats the whole page on the
logistic regression, and the interesting question is whether the two models
fail the same people.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
library(tidymodels); library(readr); library(dplyr); library(ggplot2)

diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes.csv") |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("pos", "neg")))

set.seed(123)
split <- initial_split(diabetes, prop = 0.7, strata = diabetes)
train <- training(split); test <- testing(split)

rf_fit <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |>
  set_engine("ranger", seed = 123) |>
  set_mode("classification") |>
  fit(diabetes ~ ., data = train)

pred <- augment(rf_fit, test)

# every metric in one place, and the two counts that have to travel with them
metrics_in <- function(d) {
  tibble(n     = nrow(d),
         cases = sum(d$diabetes == "pos"),
         sens  = if (any(d$diabetes == "pos")) sens_vec(d$diabetes, d$.pred_class) else NA_real_,
         spec  = if (any(d$diabetes == "neg")) spec_vec(d$diabetes, d$.pred_class) else NA_real_,
         auc   = if (n_distinct(d$diabetes) == 2) roc_auc_vec(d$diabetes, d$.pred_pos) else NA_real_)
}

by_group <- function(d, col) {
  d |> group_by(group = .data[[col]]) |> group_modify(~ metrics_in(.x)) |> ungroup()
}

metrics_in(pred)
```

## Python

```{python}
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import recall_score, roc_auc_score

diabetes = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
X = diabetes.drop(columns="diabetes")
y = (diabetes["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3,
                                          random_state=123, stratify=y)

rf_fit = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, random_state=123).fit(X_tr, y_tr)

pred = X_te.copy()
pred["truth"] = y_te
pred["pred"]  = rf_fit.predict(X_te)
pred["prob"]  = rf_fit.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]

# every metric in one place, and the two counts that have to travel with them
def metrics_in(d):
    t, yhat, p = d["truth"].values, d["pred"].values, d["prob"].values
    return pd.Series({
        "n": len(t), "cases": int(t.sum()),
        "sens": recall_score(t, yhat) if t.sum() else np.nan,
        "spec": recall_score(1 - t, 1 - yhat) if (1 - t).sum() else np.nan,
        "auc":  roc_auc_score(t, p) if 0 < t.sum() < len(t) else np.nan})

def by_group(d, col):
    return pd.DataFrame({g: metrics_in(sub)
                         for g, sub in d.groupby(col, observed=True)}).T

metrics_in(pred).round(3)
```
:::

One row, 231 patients, 84 of them with diabetes. R's split gives a sensitivity
of 0.54 and an AUC of 0.82; Python's gives 0.63 and 0.77. That row is the only
performance statement the booklet has made so far, and a commissioner reading
it has no way to tell whether it describes everybody equally.

::: {.callout-note}
## `cases`, not just `n`
`metrics_in()` returns two counts, and the second one is the one people forget.
Sensitivity is computed only on the patients who have the disease, so a group
of 63 women containing 8 cases gives you a sensitivity estimated from 8
observations, however reassuring the 63 looks in the table.
:::

## Task 1 — Split the test set, and report the gap

Cut the test set two ways — by age band and by number of pregnancies — and
compute the three metrics inside each band. Report, for each grouping, the
distance between the best and the worst group, with the group sizes beside it.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.

pred <- pred |>
  mutate(age_band  = cut(age, c(-Inf, 30, 40, 50, Inf), right = FALSE,
                         labels = c("21-29", "30-39", "40-49", "50+")),
         preg_band = ______(pregnant, c(-Inf, 1, 3, 6, Inf), right = FALSE,
                            labels = c("0", "1-2", "3-5", "6+")))

by_age  <- by_group(pred, ______)
by_preg <- by_group(pred, "preg_band")
by_age
by_preg

gap_sens <- max(by_age$sens) - ______(by_age$sens)
cat("age bands - gap in sensitivity:", round(gap_sens, 3),
    " specificity:", round(max(by_age$spec) - min(by_age$spec), 3),
    " AUC:",         round(max(by_age$auc)  - min(by_age$auc),  3), "\n")

check_metric_range(gap_sens, 0, 1, "sensitivity gap")
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
Both languages have one function that turns a numeric column into bands with
labels you choose; in R it is base, in Python it lives in `pandas`. The gap is
the range of a column, so `max()` and `min()` are all you need — and if your
answer comes back as a missing value, one band had only one class in it, which
`check_metric_range()` will tell you by failing.
:::

The age table is the kind of table that gets into a slide deck. In R the 40–49
band has a sensitivity of 0.73 against 0.46 for the under-30s; in Python the
over-50s sit at 0.46 against 0.82 for the 40–49s. Before reading anything into
either, look at the `n` and `cases` columns.

## Task 2 — How large a gap does chance produce?

The honest question is not whether the groups differ. With four groups and 231
rows they will always differ. The question is whether they differ by more than
they would if there were nothing to find.

Build the comparison the only way that needs no assumptions: shuffle the band
labels among the test rows, so the groups keep their sizes and lose their
meaning, recompute the gap, and do it a thousand times. That distribution is
the noise floor.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")

set.seed(123)
null_gaps <- replicate(1000, {
  shuffled <- pred |> mutate(age_band = ______(age_band))
  g <- by_group(shuffled, "age_band")
  max(g$sens) - min(g$sens)
})

round(quantile(null_gaps, c(0.5, 0.95)), 3)
check_gap_vs_noise(______, null_gaps, "sensitivity gap across age bands")
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
source("checks/checks.R")

set.seed(123)
null_gaps <- replicate(1000, {
  shuffled <- pred |> mutate(age_band = sample(age_band))
  g <- by_group(shuffled, "age_band")
  max(g$sens) - min(g$sens)
})

round(quantile(null_gaps, c(0.5, 0.95)), 3)
check_gap_vs_noise(gap_sens, null_gaps, "sensitivity gap across age bands")
```
:::
:::

```{python}
#| eval: false

import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *

rng = np.random.default_rng(123)
shuffled, null_gaps = pred.copy(), []
for _ in range(1000):
    shuffled["age_band"] = rng.______(pred["age_band"].values)
    g = by_group(shuffled, "age_band")
```

```{python}
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *

rng = np.random.default_rng(123)
shuffled, null_gaps = pred.copy(), []
for _ in range(1000):
    shuffled["age_band"] = rng.permutation(pred["age_band"].values)
    g = by_group(shuffled, "age_band")
    null_gaps.append(g["sens"].max() - g["sens"].min())
null_gaps = np.array(null_gaps)

print(np.quantile(null_gaps, [0.5, 0.95]).round(3))
check_gap_vs_noise(gap_sens, null_gaps, "sensitivity gap across age bands")
```
:::
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
Shuffling a column is one function call: in R it is the same function you use
to draw a sample, called with no size argument; in Python it is a method of the
random generator you have already created. Nothing else in the loop changes.

A `[fix]` from `check_gap_vs_noise()` is a result, not a bug. Read its detail
line before you touch the code.
:::

`check_gap_vs_noise()` reports the observed gap, the median of the permuted
gaps, their 95th centile and a permutation p-value. For the age bands it fails,
in both languages: the gap in sensitivity across age is 0.28 in R against a
median permuted gap of 0.28, and 0.36 in Python against a median of 0.26. Made-up
groups of the same sizes produce a gap this large about half the time in R and
about a fifth of the time in Python.

## A second grouping, where the answer is different

Run the same two steps on the pregnancy bands. This is a worked example, not a
task: the code is Task 1's and Task 2's with one column name changed, so
it is written out here in full.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3
preg <- pred |>
  mutate(preg_band = cut(pregnant, c(-Inf, 1, 3, 6, Inf), right = FALSE,
                         labels = c("0", "1-2", "3-5", "6+")))
by_preg <- by_group(preg, "preg_band")
by_preg

gap_preg <- max(by_preg$sens) - min(by_preg$sens)

set.seed(123)
null_preg <- replicate(1000, {
  g <- by_group(mutate(preg, preg_band = sample(preg_band)), "preg_band")
  max(g$sens) - min(g$sens)
})

check_gap_vs_noise(gap_preg, null_preg, "sensitivity gap across pregnancy bands")

ggplot(tibble(gap = null_preg), aes(gap)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "grey80", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = gap_preg, linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "sensitivity gap between four groups of the same sizes, labels shuffled",
       y = "permutations",
       title = "The noise floor, and the gap we observed (vertical line)")
```

## Python

```{python}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3
preg = pred.copy()
preg["preg_band"] = pd.cut(preg["pregnant"], [0, 1, 3, 6, np.inf], right=False,
                           labels=["0", "1-2", "3-5", "6+"])
by_preg = by_group(preg, "preg_band")
print(by_preg.round(3))

gap_preg = by_preg["sens"].max() - by_preg["sens"].min()

rng = np.random.default_rng(123)
shuffled, null_preg = preg.copy(), []
for _ in range(1000):
    shuffled["preg_band"] = rng.permutation(preg["preg_band"].values)
    g = by_group(shuffled, "preg_band")
    null_preg.append(g["sens"].max() - g["sens"].min())
null_preg = np.array(null_preg)

check_gap_vs_noise(gap_preg, null_preg, "sensitivity gap across pregnancy bands")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3))
ax.hist(null_preg, bins=30, color="0.8", edgecolor="white")
ax.axvline(gap_preg, color="black", lw=1.5)
ax.set_xlabel("sensitivity gap between four groups of the same sizes, labels shuffled")
ax.set_ylabel("permutations")
ax.set_title("The noise floor, and the gap we observed (vertical line)")
fig.tight_layout()
```
:::

This one clears the floor: a gap of 0.54 in R against a 95th centile of 0.46
(p = 0.03), and 0.60 in Python against 0.47 (p = 0.01). Hold on to it until the
end of the page, because the group driving it is the one with six or eight
cases in it.

## Task 3 — Put an interval on every group

A p-value for the gap does not tell a service how good the model is for the
over-50s. For that you need an interval around each group's own estimate.
Resample the rows within a band, with replacement, recompute sensitivity, and
take the 2.5th and 97.5th centiles.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
boot_sens <- function(d, B = 1000) {
  v <- replicate(B, {
    i <- sample(nrow(d), replace = ______)
    if (any(d$diabetes[i] == "pos")) sens_vec(d$diabetes[i], d$.pred_class[i]) else NA_real_
  })
  quantile(v, c(0.025, ______), na.rm = TRUE)
}

set.seed(123)
intervals <- lapply(levels(pred$age_band), function(g) {
  d  <- dplyr::filter(pred, age_band == g)
  ci <- boot_sens(d)
  tibble(group = g, n = nrow(d), cases = sum(d$diabetes == "pos"),
         sens  = sens_vec(d$diabetes, d$.pred_class),
         lo = ci[[1]], hi = ci[[2]], width = ci[[2]] - ci[[1]])
}) |> bind_rows()
intervals

cat("widest interval:", intervals$group[which.max(intervals$width)],
    "| smallest band:", intervals$group[which.min(intervals$n)],
    "| lowest AUC:",    as.character(by_age$group[which.min(by_age$auc)]), "\n")
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3
boot_sens <- function(d, B = 1000) {
  v <- replicate(B, {
    i <- sample(nrow(d), replace = TRUE)
    if (any(d$diabetes[i] == "pos")) sens_vec(d$diabetes[i], d$.pred_class[i]) else NA_real_
  })
  quantile(v, c(0.025, 0.975), na.rm = TRUE)
}

set.seed(123)
intervals <- lapply(levels(pred$age_band), function(g) {
  d  <- dplyr::filter(pred, age_band == g)
  ci <- boot_sens(d)
  tibble(group = g, n = nrow(d), cases = sum(d$diabetes == "pos"),
         sens  = sens_vec(d$diabetes, d$.pred_class),
         lo = ci[[1]], hi = ci[[2]], width = ci[[2]] - ci[[1]])
}) |> bind_rows()
intervals

cat("widest interval:", intervals$group[which.max(intervals$width)],
    "| smallest band:", intervals$group[which.min(intervals$n)],
    "| lowest AUC:",    as.character(by_age$group[which.min(by_age$auc)]), "\n")

ggplot(intervals, aes(x = sens, y = group)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), orientation = "y", width = 0.15) +
  geom_point(aes(size = cases)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = sens_vec(pred$diabetes, pred$.pred_class), linetype = 2) +
  labs(x = "sensitivity (dashed line: all 231 test rows)", y = NULL, size = "cases",
       title = "Sensitivity by age band, with 95% bootstrap intervals")
```
:::
:::

## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
def boot_sens(d, rng, B=1000):
    t, yhat = d["truth"].values, d["pred"].values
    v = [recall_score(t[i], yhat[i]) if t[i].sum() else np.nan
         for i in (rng.integers(0, len(d), ______) for _ in range(B))]
    return np.nanquantile(v, [0.025, ______])

rng = np.random.default_rng(123)
rows = []
for g, d in pred.groupby("age_band", observed=True):
    lo, hi = boot_sens(d, rng)
    rows.append({"group": g, "n": len(d), "cases": int(d["truth"].sum()),
                 "sens": recall_score(d["truth"], d["pred"]),
                 "lo": lo, "hi": hi, "width": hi - lo})
intervals = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(intervals.round(3))

print("widest interval:", intervals.loc[intervals["width"].idxmax(), "group"],
      "| smallest band:", intervals.loc[intervals["n"].idxmin(), "group"],
      "| lowest AUC:",    by_age["auc"].idxmin())
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3
def boot_sens(d, rng, B=1000):
    t, yhat = d["truth"].values, d["pred"].values
    v = [recall_score(t[i], yhat[i]) if t[i].sum() else np.nan
         for i in (rng.integers(0, len(d), len(d)) for _ in range(B))]
    return np.nanquantile(v, [0.025, 0.975])

rng = np.random.default_rng(123)
rows = []
for g, d in pred.groupby("age_band", observed=True):
    lo, hi = boot_sens(d, rng)
    rows.append({"group": g, "n": len(d), "cases": int(d["truth"].sum()),
                 "sens": recall_score(d["truth"], d["pred"]),
                 "lo": lo, "hi": hi, "width": hi - lo})
intervals = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(intervals.round(3))

print("widest interval:", intervals.loc[intervals["width"].idxmax(), "group"],
      "| smallest band:", intervals.loc[intervals["n"].idxmin(), "group"],
      "| lowest AUC:",    by_age["auc"].idxmin())

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3))
ax.errorbar(intervals["sens"], intervals["group"],
            xerr=[intervals["sens"] - intervals["lo"],
                  intervals["hi"] - intervals["sens"]],
            fmt="o", capsize=3, color="black")
ax.axvline(recall_score(pred["truth"], pred["pred"]), ls="--", color="grey")
ax.set_xlabel("sensitivity (dashed line: all 231 test rows)")
ax.set_title("Sensitivity by age band, with 95% bootstrap intervals")
fig.tight_layout()
```
:::
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
A bootstrap resample is the same size as the group it came from, drawn with
replacement — that is the whole idea, and it is one argument in R and one
argument in Python. The upper centile is whatever makes the interval symmetric
around 95%.
:::

## The result that should bother you

The over-50s are the worst-served group in this test set. In R their AUC of
0.73 is the lowest of the four bands; in Python their AUC of 0.45 is the lowest
of the four and below chance, which would mean the forest is worse than a coin
for women over 50. They are also the band a service would most want to get
right.

Three steps.

1. The over-50s band has 19 rows in R and 23 in Python, of which 11 are cases
   in both. It is the smallest band, it has the widest bootstrap interval of
   the four — 0.33 to 0.90 in R, 0.17 to 0.75 in Python — and the width of that
   interval, around 0.57 to 0.58, is larger than the entire gap between the
   best and worst band that we set out to interpret. The smallest group gets
   the most extreme point estimate because it has the fewest cases to average
   over, and the same thinness is what makes the estimate extreme and what
   makes it uncertain.
2. The direction is not stable either. The same band, the same model
   specification, the same seed: in R the over-50s have a sensitivity of 0.64,
   above the overall 0.54, and in Python 0.46, below the overall 0.63. The only
   difference between the two is which rows landed in the test set. A
   worst-served group that changes places when you reshuffle the split is a
   property of the split.
3. Permuting the labels says the same thing without any of the interpretation.
   Four made-up age bands of the same sizes produce a sensitivity gap of 0.28
   or more in half of a thousand permutations, and the observed gap is 0.28. A
   difference smaller than the noise floor is not a finding, and ranking the
   bands by sensitivity is then an elaborate way of ranking them by size.

The pregnancy grouping is the useful counter-case, and it is only half a
counter-case. That gap does clear the floor (p = 0.03 in R, p = 0.01 in
Python), so something there is not chance. Then look at which band is driving
it: the women with one or two pregnancies, sensitivity 0.25 in R and 0.17 in
Python — estimated from 8 cases and 6 cases respectively, inside a group of 63
and 57 rows. Repeat Task 3 on the pregnancy bands and that band's interval runs from
0.00 upwards. So even the gap
that survives the permutation test rests on single-digit event counts, and we
have looked at six gaps on this page — two groupings by three metrics — while
testing two of them. A p-value of 0.03 is not a licence when the search was
that wide.

## What this cannot be evidence of

::: {.callout-important}
## The method is real; the finding is not
A subgroup gap measured on 231 test rows of a teaching extract is not evidence
about any service. The smallest age band here holds eleven cases — few enough
that a gap of the size you are about to find can be produced by chance alone —
and no sentence of the form "the model under-serves group X" can be carried out
of this chapter.

That is not a reason to skip the exercise; it is the exercise. Someone auditing
a deployed model for equity has to be able to tell a disparity from an artefact
of the data they were handed, and the only way to practise is on data where you
already know the answer. What you would need to make a real claim is nameable:
data from the service you are auditing, with the subgroup actually recorded
rather than inferred; a list of subgroups written down before anyone looks at a
metric; and enough cases in each of them — events, not rows — that the interval
is narrower than the difference you would act on. On this page the third
condition fails by a factor of several for every band.
:::

## Reflection

1. Your service wants a dashboard with one sensitivity per age band. Write the
   sentence you would put under the table so that a reader cannot misread a
   small group as a failing one. It should be a sentence, not a number.
2. Where does the list of subgroups come from? You cannot search the data for
   the grouping with the largest gap and then report that gap — explain why
   not, and say who should decide the list instead.
3. Suppose the over-50s disparity were real. Name two responses a service could
   make that are not "retrain the model", and say what evidence would tell you
   which to choose.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Answers.** (1) Anything that puts the event count and the interval in the
reader's eye — for example, that each band's sensitivity is estimated from the
cases in that band only, that the smallest band's interval spans more than half
the scale, and that the bands cannot be ranked on these data. (2) From the
service, the population and the regulatory context, before the analysis:
protected characteristics, groups known to be under-served, groups the model
will actually be used on. Searching for the largest gap is multiple testing
with the multiplicity hidden, and this page shows the machinery — the maximum
gap over four random bands has a distribution with a median of about 0.26 to
0.28, so
the largest of several searched gaps is almost guaranteed to look impressive.
(3) Candidates: a different threshold for that group (@sec-thresholds), extra
human review of its negatives, restricting the model's licensed population to
the groups it was validated in, or collecting more data before deploying at
all. Which one depends on the cost of a missed case versus a false alarm in
that group, and on whether the group's own members would accept a different
rule being applied to them.

**Expected values.** Both splits, seed 123. Quote ranges; the forest is
stochastic and the bootstrap moves the last digit.

| | R (ranger) | Python (sklearn) |
|---|---|---|
| test set | 231 rows, 84 cases | 231 rows, 84 cases |
| overall sens / spec / AUC | 0.54 / 0.85 / 0.82 | 0.63 / 0.75 / 0.77 |
| age bands, n | 136 / 43 / 33 / 19 | 131 / 41 / 36 / 23 |
| age bands, cases | 35 / 23 / 15 / 11 | 32 / 19 / 22 / 11 |
| gap in sens / spec / AUC by age | 0.28 / 0.44 / 0.10 | 0.36 / 0.50 / 0.35 |
| permuted age gap: median, 95th | 0.28, 0.55 | 0.26, 0.50 |
| p for the age gap | 0.45–0.55 | 0.18–0.25 |
| gap in sens by pregnancies | 0.54 | 0.60 |
| p for the pregnancy gap | 0.02–0.04 | 0.005–0.02 |
| widest 95% interval (50+) | 0.33–0.90 | 0.17–0.75 |

: {tbl-colwidths="[34,33,33]"}

The 40–49 band is the most extreme in R (sensitivity 0.73) and the over-50s in
Python (0.46); in both languages the two smallest bands hold the two most
extreme estimates, which is the point.

**Common failures.** (1) Computing the gap on a column containing `NA`, because
a band had one class only — `max()` returns `NA` and the check fails with the
class printed rather than a number; this is worth letting happen. (2) Reading a
`[fix]` from `check_gap_vs_noise()` as a broken answer. Say in advance that the
expected result is a failure and that the detail line is the output. (3)
Permuting the outcome instead of the group label, which tests something else
entirely — if someone does it, it is a good two minutes. (4) Bootstrapping the
whole test set rather than within the band, which gives every band almost the
same interval. (5) Expecting the two languages to agree on which band is worst.
They do not, and that is step 2 of the argument.

**Timing.** The permutations are about seven seconds in R and eight in Python
for a thousand; the bootstrap is faster. If you are behind, set the loops to
200 and keep all three tasks — the p-values move in the second decimal and no
conclusion changes. Do not drop Task 2 to save Task 3: the noise floor is the
reason this page exists.
:::
:::

## Stretch

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 1 — Do the two models fail the same people?
Repeat the whole page on the logistic regression of @sec-logistic-regression,
fitted to the same training rows. Put its subgroup table next to the forest's.
If the two models disagree about which band is worst served, what does that
tell you about the disparity — and what would it take for them to agree for the
right reason rather than by chance?
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 2 — How many cases would you need?
Keep the model and simulate the audit you wish you could run. Draw groups of
25, 50, 100 and 400 cases by resampling the test set, and record how often a
true sensitivity difference of 0.10 between two groups is detectable at all.
The answer tells you the minimum size of a subgroup worth reporting, and it is
larger than anything on this page.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 3 — A threshold per group
@sec-thresholds chose one threshold for everybody. Choose one per age band so
that every band reaches the same sensitivity, and report what it costs in
specificity and in extra referrals. Then write the paragraph you would have to
put in front of a clinical governance committee to justify applying a different
rule to patients of different ages.
:::

## What you can and cannot now claim

**Can:** that you can compute a model's performance inside subgroups of a test
set, report each estimate with the number of cases behind it and a bootstrap
interval around it, and build a permutation noise floor that says whether a
between-group gap is larger than chance produces. That is the whole machinery
of a fairness audit's measurement step, and it is not difficult.

**Cannot:** that this model under-serves anybody. The test set has 231 rows, the
smallest band has 11 cases, and the one gap that cleared the noise floor was
driven by a group with six. What you have practised is the arithmetic and the
discipline of reporting it; the claim itself needs a service's own data, a
prespecified subgroup list and event counts an order of magnitude larger. An
estimate reported without uncertainty is not an estimate — the same point this
page makes about people rather than about variables.
